atoms.text: General elections follow the first-past-the-post voting system, also called first-preference plurality. The candidate for MP of a constituency with the most votes wins, even if the majority of voters did not prefer this candidate. This happens because voters may only choose their first priority.

atoms.b: In the above results of a general election in a constituency, the winner is the candidate for the ((++Labour Conservative Liberal_Democratic)) party.

The candidate won with ((++34% 24% 12%)) of the votes, although 66% of voters did not vote for them. But because these votes are ((++split_among_several_parties all_cast_for_the_same_party)), their preferences are irrelevant.

atoms.text: The result is that most people tend to vote for either Labour or the Conservatives. Since World War II, the leading party has always been one of the two.

The Labour Party is a centre-left UK political party founded in 1900. Their ideals are more liberal, concentrating on equal rights and social welfare. Labour advocates for government regulations in the market as well as reduced taxes for those earning less money. Typical voters are usually from the working class, especially in cities and industrial areas in the North.

The Conservative and Unionist Party is a centre-right UK political party that emerged from the Tory Party in 1834. They favour a free market and low taxes for businesses and people with high incomes. Their voters are most often from the upper and middle class living in the countryside and the rich Southern areas. The Conservatives focus more on individual rights rather than community, but they strongly support a unified UK.

hint.text:
The Tories and the Whigs were the UK's two major political parties from the late 17th to mid-19th century. The Tory Party eventually became the Conservative Party, and the Whigs the Liberal Party.
In the 1950s, most Liberal voters started favouring the Labour Party instead. Since then, the Liberal Party has not been able to regain its former influence.
